summary: A cover note for the Telnet protocol specification and Telnet option specifications produced at a UCLA meeting on March 5, 1973, with a long list of attendees. It presents them as the official Telnet protocol, subject to comment. It obsoletes RFC 158 and was updated by RFC 562.

eli5.summary: After lots of arguing, a group met and wrote down the rules for typing into a faraway computer, which everyone was asked to follow.

subtitle: The cover note that announced a new official TELNET specification and a phase-in schedule for it.

tldr.problem: After much discussion of TELNET in the RFC series, the community needed one agreed specification and a plan for moving from the old command forms to the new ones.
tldr.mechanism: An open meeting at UCLA on 5 March produced two attached documents, a TELNET Protocol Specification and a set of TELNET Option Specifications, plus two dates for phasing in the new commands.
tldr.outcome: The attached documents were to be viewed as the official TELNET Protocol. The index lists RFC 495 as obsoleting RFC 158 and as updated by RFC 562.

today: The index lists RFC 495 as obsoleting RFC 158 and as updated by RFC 562, and its status is recorded as unknown. It is a cover note, and the attached specifications are what it announces.

sections.title: The Meeting and Its Documents
sections.content:
Alex McKenzie of BBN reports that an open meeting at UCLA on 5 March formulated a new specification for the TELNET Protocol. It was co-chaired by McKenzie and Jon Postel, and the RFC lists the attendees.

Two attached documents carry the results: the TELNET Protocol Specification (NIC #15372) and the TELNET Option Specifications (NIC #15373). The attendees reviewed them, and they should be viewed as the official TELNET Protocol, though still subject to minor revisions. Comments go to McKenzie at the NIC.
sections.eli5: A room full of experts agreed on the rulebook. This note is the cover page, and the rulebook is attached.

sections.title: Phasing In the New Commands
sections.content:
There are two key dates. After the first, sites can send the new form of TELNET commands and special codes without expecting error responses. After the second, sites may remove the code that handles the old form. In between, sites gradually implement and test an interpreter for the new commands.

The meeting felt that lead times of about 60 and 260 days were appropriate, so the dates are set at 1 July 1973 and 1 January 1974.
sections.eli5: Everyone gets time to switch. First a date after which the new words are safe to use, and a later date after which the old words can be dropped.

sections.title: The Option Specifications
sections.content:
The attached options allow negotiation of binary transmission, echoing, reconnection, suppression of "Go Ahead", approximate message size, use of a "timing mark", discussion of status and extension of the option code set. They were prepared by Dave Walden with help from several others, by Jerry Burchfiel and by David Crocker. Together they appear to cover most capabilities of the current TELNET, except "Hide Your Input."

Walden also promised to specify NVT printer line width, NVT printer page size and the mapping between a terminal's line terminator and the NVT characters to be transmitted, and intended to seek collaboration on an EBCDIC option. The RFC stresses that announcing intent to write an option is not an exclusive right to it.
sections.eli5: Besides the main rules there is a menu of extras that two computers can agree to use, like echoing what you type, and more extras were promised.
